web_evidence.title: Perennial Favorites Sampler — The Paris Wife excerpt
web_evidence.note: The authorized publisher excerpt begins with Hadley’s sustained retrospective first-person narration.

web_evidence.title: The Paris Wife Reader’s Guide
web_evidence.note: The publisher-hosted guide says most of the book is in Hadley's voice and that select passages present Ernest's perspective, but perspective and voice do not by themselves identify grammatical person. It is a credible contextual description, not direct ALTERNATING-person evidence.

web_evidence.title: Paula McLain Writing Styles in The Paris Wife: A Novel
web_evidence.note: The explicit POV analysis identifies Hadley’s first-person past narration as the majority mode and describes switches to third-person narration in key chapters, including Chapters 18 and 27.

web_evidence.title: The Paris Wife Prologue–Chapter 11 Summary & Analysis
web_evidence.note: The structural analysis identifies Hadley’s retrospective first-person prologue and a sustained third-person chapter centered on Ernest within the opening section.

web_evidence.title: The Paris Wife Chapters 12–23 Summary & Analysis
web_evidence.note: The analysis explicitly identifies Chapter 18 as a third-person Ernest section, corroborating that the shift recurs beyond the opening.

web_evidence.title: (Don’t) Forget Paris: An Interview with Author Paula McLain
web_evidence.note: McLain confirms that she chose first person from Hadley’s point of view; this supports the dominant strand but does not address the novel’s documented Ernest interludes.

person_note: Hadley's retrospective first-person narration controls most of the novel, as shown repeatedly by the Goodreads passages and the authorized opening. However, this is not merely a first-person novel containing isolated dialogue: multiple sustained Goodreads passages narrate Ernest externally in third person while accessing his private thoughts, and independent Tier C structural sources identify recurring third-person chapters, including Chapters 18 and 27. The publisher guide corroborates that select passages shift to Ernest's perspective, but it does not name their grammatical person and therefore does not itself support ALTERNATING. Under the methodology, sustained base sections in different persons require ALTERNATING even though first person predominates. Confidence is med because the Tier A prose establishes only the first-person opening and the alternating structure depends on diagnostic Goodreads passages plus Tier C study-guide analysis. Audit: independent review retained ALTERNATING, corrected the publisher guide from Tier A/ALTERNATING to Tier C/none, and downgraded high to med.
